title: Food & drink
goal: Order food and drink, say what you want and don't want, talk about tastes and say what you like.
intro:
Telugu food is famous across India for being **spicy**: Andhra chilli, tangy tamarind, pickles and *pappu* (dal) with rice and ghee. A Telugu meal centres on *అన్నం* (cooked rice) with a series of curries, *pappu*, *chāru* (rasam) and *perugu* (curd) to finish.

Grammatically, wanting and liking are expressed with the **dative**: not 'I want coffee' but 'to me coffee is needed' (*నాకు కాఫీ కావాలి*).

vocab.note: To eat a meal: భోజనం చేయు.

phrases.en: One plate of idli and one coffee.
Will you have tea or coffee?
Shall I serve you a bit more rice?

grammar.title: 'I want': dative + కావాలి
grammar.body:
Telugu expresses wanting and needing with the **dative case**: the person who wants is marked with **-కు/-కి** (-ku/-ki), and the verb is **కావాలి** (kāvāli, 'is needed'), which never changes:
నాకు (nāku) to me · నీకు (nīku) to you · మీకు (mīku) to you (pol.) · అతనికి (ataniki) to him · ఆమెకు (āmeku) to her · మాకు (māku) / మనకు (manaku) to us · వాళ్ళకి (vāḷḷaki) to them

The opposite is **వద్దు** (vaddu, 'not wanted'). As a question, add -ā: *కావాలా?* (do you want?).

examples.en: We'd like two plates of idli.

grammar.title: 'I like': ఇష్టం and నచ్చు
grammar.body:
Liking also takes the dative subject. **నాకు X ఇష్టం** (nāku X iṣṭam) = I like X (in general, a lasting preference). To say you *love* something, use **X అంటే ఇష్టం**: *నాకు బిర్యానీ అంటే చాలా ఇష్టం*. Negative: **ఇష్టం లేదు**.

**నచ్చు** (nachchu, 'to please') is used for a specific experience: *ఈ కూర నాకు నచ్చింది* (I liked this curry, lit. this curry pleased me). Negative: **నచ్చలేదు**.

The same pattern gives hunger and thirst: *నాకు ఆకలిగా ఉంది* (I'm hungry, lit. to me it is hungrily).

examples.en: Did you like the Telugu food?

dialogue.title: At the tiffin centre
dialogue.setting: Mr Varma orders breakfast at a busy tiffin centre in Vijayawada.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.en: Come in, sir, what would you like?

lines.speaker: Varma
lines.native: ఒక మసాలా దోసె, ఒక ప్లేట్ ఇడ్లీ ఇవ్వండి.
lines.roman: oka masālā dōse, oka plēṭ iḍlī ivvaṇḍi.
lines.en: One masala dosa and one plate of idli, please.

lines.speaker: Varma
lines.native: చాలా బాగుంది! కానీ చట్నీ కొంచెం కారంగా ఉంది.
lines.roman: chālā bāgundi! kānī chaṭnī konchem kāraṅgā undi.
lines.en: Very good! But the chutney is a bit spicy.

lines.speaker: Varma
lines.en: No, that's enough. The bill, please.

culture: *భోజనం చేశారా?* ('Have you eaten?') is as much a greeting as a question, and a guest will be urged to eat more than once; saying *చాలు* or *వద్దండి* firmly (often with a hand over the plate) is how you stop the second and third helpings. Traditional meals are served on a banana leaf and eaten with the right hand. Telugu cuisine is known for *gongura* (sorrel) pickle, *pesarattu* (green-gram dosa) and Hyderabadi *biryani*.
